1.point: The remembering we lose and the rules we keep are one religion at different depths, so there is no path outside the law; this chapter will show why.
steps: The chapter's quotation asks for remembering God and keeping His commands together.
In our own prayer the two come apart: the form is valid in law while the mind wanders.
That gap tempts the conclusion that the rules are an outer layer the traveller can shed.
Most masters taught the opposite; the chapter will show the law is the only way in and is kept to the end.

2.point: The path and the truth are the inside of the law's own acts, so they can only be reached by going through the law.
steps: Define the law: the outward acts and their conditions of validity.
Define the path as the way from the law to nearness, and the truth as what is seen at the end of the path.
Show the path is not a second set of acts: two outwardly identical prayers are both valid, the jurist can judge only the form.
What differs is the inward manner of the same act; that inward manner is the path, and what is seen through it is the truth.
So the three are one reality at three depths: shell, core, kernel.
The dependence runs one way: law without path is possible, path without law is not, because the path has nothing else to work on.
Therefore each depth is reached only through the one before (ship, sea, pearl).

3.point: No wonder-working and no inner experience can substitute for keeping the law.
steps: From the ship image: whoever claims the truth while dropping even one command is a liar.
The lie is not in the feat, which may be real, but in the claim; the feat is magic, not karama.
Why the law cannot be bypassed: law produces good character, and good character is the only way into knowledge of God.
So someone who claims to be beyond the law has broken the first link of the chain that leads to knowledge.
What arrives without the law is a counterfeit easily mistaken for knowledge of God (the forty-day exercise).
Even genuine experiences on the true path are preliminaries; what counts is a lasting change in the self.
Only the unbroken, lifelong practice of the law produces that lasting change; a forty-day exercise ends.

4.point: The inner work does not start outside the law but inside the prayer already prayed, by bringing attention to its words.
steps: The first inner work is done inside the prayer, beginning with knowing what Allahu akbar means.
Knowing what we say needs attention, and attention cannot be forced by will.
The difficulty is a circle: saying the words from the heart needs knowledge that comes only from practising the words with the very attention that keeps slipping.
The faculty of attention is not missing (a book holds it); what is missing is the habit of bringing it to prayer.
That habit is built inside the law, by degrees, through the means Khomeini names.

5.point: The law binds the traveller to the very end; arrival changes only why it is kept, from growth to gratitude.
steps: The claim that high stations release the traveller from the law exists and the Kernel rejects it outright.
Proof: the Prophet, who went furthest, kept every precept to the last moments of his life.
The error comes from misunderstanding the stages of worship; the unveiled keep the law more, not less.
The one true sense of 'stages': worship moves the soul from potentiality to actuality, so for a perfected soul it is no longer for growth; what changes is the reason, not the law.
The reason is gratitude, in the Prophet's own answer, which is also what the chapter's opening quotation asks for.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Places the quotation and draws out its pairing of remembering God with keeping His commands, which the whole chapter turns on.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Shows the pairing coming apart in our own prayer (valid in law, mind elsewhere); this is the hook and the gap the chapter addresses.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: States the tempting wrong conclusion drawn from that gap, the position the chapter refutes.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: States the chapter's thesis in the terms of the title: no path outside the law, one religion at different depths, law kept to the end.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Defines the first of the three terms, the law, as the outward acts and their validity.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Defines the path as the way from law to nearness and the truth as what the path arrives at.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Supplies the key step that the path is not a second set of acts: two identical outward prayers are both valid and the jurist can judge only the form.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Completes the step: what differs is the inward manner of the same act, which is the path; what is seen through it is the truth. Khomeini's valid/accepted line supports it. The outward frame remains the law.

¶9.label: support
¶9.why: The Prophet's words/actions/states give the primary-source basis for the mapping ¶8 just drew and for ¶10's 'one reality seen from different sides' (one person, three aspects). Borderline: ¶10 would still read without it.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Draws the inference: the three are not separate roads but one reality at three depths, and names the shell/core/kernel scheme the section is titled after. The Mutahhari bracket is a second voice saying the same and could go.

¶11.label: aside
¶11.why: A second illustration that one salah holds all three depths; ¶8 already showed this with the Prophet's prayer and ¶10 already stated the one-reality claim. Bahmanpour's sentence repeats ¶8. Nothing later depends on khidma/qurb/wusul.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Supplies the one-way dependence: law without path is possible, path without law is not, because the path is the inside of the law's own acts. Amuli's rule supports it.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Lands the section's conclusion (each depth only through the one before, none skipped) and introduces the ship/sea/pearl image that ¶14 argues from.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Applies the ship image to the person who claims the truth without the law: Kubra's test, 'liars'. The first step of the section.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Needed to prevent misreading 'liars': the feat may be real, the lie is the claim, so the feat is magic not karama. Without this the test looks like a denial of the feats.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Supplies the reason the law cannot be bypassed: Bahari's order, law as the means to good character, good character as the way to knowledge of God.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Draws the inference from Bahari's order to the claimant beyond the law: they have broken the first link. The middle sentences re-run ¶16's order in reverse and could be trimmed, but the application is new.

¶18.label: restate
¶18.why: The paragraph itself says Khomeini 'reaches the same conclusion' as ¶17: without the law, no knowledge of God. A second authority for a step already made. ¶19 borrows the word 'light' from it, but that hook could be reworded; no step depends on this paragraph.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: New step: what does arrive without the law is a counterfeit easily taken for knowledge of God (the forty-day remark).

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: New step: even genuine experiences on the true path are preliminaries; what counts is a lasting change in the self.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Closes the section: only unbroken lifelong practice of the law produces that lasting change, so the real ʿarif is the one who keeps it continuously. Picks up the forty-day remark to make the contrast, not to repeat it.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Opens the section's step: the first inner work happens inside the prayer, beginning with knowing what Allahu akbar means.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: Supplies the obstacle: knowing what we say needs attention, and attention cannot be forced; the car thought returns.

¶24.label: restate
¶24.why: The cliff image dresses the claim already made in ¶23 (presence cannot be summoned by deciding). It raises a puzzle ('logically this should not happen') but ¶25 resolves the circle without referring to the cliff, and ¶26's book example does the comparative work. Deleting it breaks nothing.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Supplies the diagnosis: a circle between knowledge, practice and attention; this is why the path is harder than the law.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: New step: the faculty of attention is not missing (a book holds it); what is missing is the habit of bringing it to prayer.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: Lands the point: the habit is built inside the law, by Khomeini's two means, a degree at a time; the forward reference to Chapter Ten is a hand-off, not a new step.

¶28.label: advance
¶28.why: States the claim of release and the Kernel's outright rejection: the law binds from first to final stage.

¶29.label: advance
¶29.why: Supplies the proof: the Prophet kept every precept to his last moments; if he was never released, no one reaches a station where the law stops.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: Repeats the Kernel's rejection of ¶28 in a second form ('hypocrite') and notes it is close to Kubra's test from ¶14. The allowance for lapses from error or forgetfulness is a qualification nothing later uses.

¶31.label: advance
¶31.why: Adds a step beyond 'still bound': the unveiled keep the forms more, and the claim of release is an error about the stages of worship, which is the hinge ¶32 turns on.

¶32.label: advance
¶32.why: Supplies the section's key distinction: worship is for growth while the soul is growing and is not for growth once perfected; what changes on arrival is the reason, not the law.

¶33.label: advance
¶33.why: Sets up the Prophet's own statement of the reason (the quotation that follows); without it the quotation hangs.

¶34.label: advance
¶34.why: Names the reason, gratitude, and closes the loop with the Munajat at the head of the chapter, which asked for exactly that.

¶35.label: aside
¶35.why: The four-journeys scheme is doctrine the point does not need. 'To the last breath' was already proved by the Prophet in ¶29 and the Kernel's 'final stage' in ¶28; ¶36 draws nothing from it. It reads as a bridge to Chapter Sixteen rather than a link in this chain.

¶36.label: restate
¶36.why: Summarises the conclusions of all four preceding sections, each of which has already been stated at its own close. By the standard that a conclusion is stated once, this paragraph adds no link.

¶37.label: aside
¶37.why: A bridge question to the next chapter; it opens a question this chapter does not answer and supplies no step toward the section's point.
